The work is the *Shōrin-zu byōbu*, the Pine Trees screens, by Hasegawa Tōhaku. It was painted in the 1590s, though the exact year is unknown. It is a designated National Treasure and is often called the greatest ink painting made in Japan. It also has a puzzle at its centre: there are good reasons to think it was never meant to be seen as a finished work.

## What is actually there

Start with the format. A *byōbu* is a folding screen made of hinged panels. Here there are two screens of six panels each, every screen roughly 1.5 metres tall and 3.5 metres wide. They were made to stand on the floor in a zigzag, as a pair, so that they could divide a room, block a draught or set a mood. The darkest of them stands in front, with its trunk drawn in a few heavy strokes and its needles in short, fast slashes of black ink. Behind and beside it, other pines are painted in progressively thinner ink: grey, then pale grey, then a tone so faint it seems to be dissolving as you look. The eye takes these differences in density as distance. The dark tree is close, the pale tree is far off, and the space between them is full of fog.

Then the trees stop and there is a stretch of empty paper. Further left a second group appears, leaning slightly, as if the wind or the slope of the ground pushed them that way. The left-hand screen repeats the pattern with variations: a group, an emptiness, another group. Near the top of the left screen, if you look carefully, there is a faint white shape that most viewers read as a distant snow-covered mountain. It is barely there at all, an outline suggested by the slightest darkening of the paper around it.

Two things repay close attention.

The first is the brushwork. Up close the needles are not delicate. They are rough, quick, almost violent strokes, with the ink splitting where the bristles separated. Some writers have suggested that Tōhaku used a worn brush or one made of straw to get this broken texture. Nobody can be certain, but the effect is clear enough. ## A gold world

To see why fog and pale ink would have looked strange in the 1590s, picture what wealthy Japanese rooms looked like at the time.

The late sixteenth century in Japan is called the Momoyama period. It was the era of the warlords Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who ended more than a century of civil war and reunified the country by force. They built castles with enormous audience halls, and they wanted those halls to overwhelm visitors. The answer was gold. Screens and sliding doors were covered in gold leaf, and on that blazing ground painters set huge trees, lions and rocks in strong mineral colours: malachite green, azurite blue, white made from crushed shell.

The master of this style was Kanō Eitoku (1543–1590), head of the Kanō school, the hereditary family workshop that dominated official painting for generations. A screen in the same museum, the *Cypress Trees* screen usually attributed to Eitoku, shows what the dominant taste looked like. A single cypress twists across the panels like a muscle. Its trunk is thick and dark, its branches lunge sideways, and the background is solid gold. It is a painting of power, built to be seen across a large hall by lamplight.

Tōhaku came from outside this world. He was born in 1539 in Nanao, on the Noto Peninsula on the Sea of Japan coast, and was adopted into a family of dyers named Hasegawa. In his early career, under the name Shinshun, he painted Buddhist images and portraits for provincial patrons, many of them connected to the Nichiren sect of Buddhism, to which his family belonged. Around 1571, in his early thirties, he moved to Kyoto. That was late to start competing in the capital, and he had no family workshop behind him.

He did it anyway, and in the next twenty years he became one of the few painters able to challenge the Kanō directly. His connections helped. Through Nichiren temples, and reportedly through the tea master Sen no Rikyū, he reached patrons at the great Zen temple of Daitoku-ji and eventually Hideyoshi himself. Sources from the period suggest that the Kanō school regarded him as a threat. One episode, recorded later and probably shaped by retelling, has the Kanō blocking a commission he hoped to get at the imperial palace around 1590.

He could paint in gold when it suited him, and he did it brilliantly. When Hideyoshi's infant son Tsurumatsu died in 1591, Hideyoshi founded a memorial temple, Shōun-ji, and Tōhaku's workshop received the commission for its wall paintings. The surviving panels are now at the temple of Chishaku-in in Kyoto. They include a great *Maple Tree* attributed to Tōhaku and a *Cherry Blossoms* attributed to his son Kyūzō. They are gold, colourful and confident, as grand as anything the Kanō produced.

So the Pine Trees screens are not the work of someone who couldn't do gold. They come from a painter who could and who, in this case, chose to leave almost everything out.

## Where the fog came from

Tōhaku's ink came from China, by way of an older Japanese tradition.

From the thirteenth century onward, Zen monks travelling between Japan and China brought back paintings in monochrome ink. One painter was valued above almost all others: the Chinese Chan (Zen) monk Muqi, active in the mid-thirteenth century, known in Japan as Mokkei. His works were treasured by Japanese collectors even though they were little regarded in China. The most famous of them is *Six Persimmons*, now at Daitoku-ji, in which six fruit sit in a row on an empty ground, painted in a few tones of ink. Daitoku-ji also holds a Muqi triptych of a white-robed Guanyin (the bodhisattva of compassion) flanked by a crane emerging from a bamboo grove and a gibbon mother holding her young in a tree. In those paintings the mist around the figures is made of untouched silk and diluted ink washes.

Tōhaku had access to Daitoku-ji, and his own work shows he studied Muqi closely. Some of his monkey paintings follow Muqi's gibbons quite directly. Muqi's method, in which forms emerge from and dissolve into the empty ground, is the clearest ancestor of the Pine Trees.

The other ancestor is Japanese. Sesshū Tōyō (1420–1506) was the great ink painter of the previous century. He had actually travelled to Ming China and came back with a sharper, more structured style. Late in life Tōhaku began signing some works as the "fifth generation from Sesshū." He had no documented teacher-to-student line connecting him to Sesshū. Historians generally read the claim as a strategy: by attaching himself to the most revered name in Japanese ink painting, the outsider gave himself a lineage to set against the Kanō family tree.

We know something of how Tōhaku thought about these models because of a short text called the *Tōhaku Gasetsu* ("Tōhaku's Talks on Painting"). It was written down by Nittsū, a Nichiren priest of the Kyoto temple Honpō-ji, from conversations with the painter. Nothing in it explains the Pine Trees screens, but it confirms that he saw himself as an heir to Muqi and Sesshū.

What he did with that inheritance was new, though. Muqi's mist surrounds a single object at the scale of a hanging scroll. Tōhaku spread it across twelve panels and made the mist the subject. The Chinese ink tradition rarely used the empty ground as the main event at that size. The Kanō screens filled every surface. The Pine Trees took the scale and format of the grand Momoyama screen and filled it mostly with nothing.

Here the story gets harder. Several pieces of physical evidence suggest the screens were not made as a finished presentation work.

**The paper.** The screens are painted on fairly ordinary, coarse paper, not the fine material you would expect for an important commission. The sheets are joined in ways that look somewhat irregular.

**The joins between panels.** In some places the composition does not run neatly across the borders between panels. Branches and groups seem slightly misaligned, as if the paintings were cut and remounted, possibly in a different order from the original.

**The seals.** The screens carry seals reading "Hasegawa" and "Tōhaku." Many specialists regard them as later additions rather than seals Tōhaku stamped himself. A dealer or later owner may have added them to make the attribution official.

What we have would then be a working draft that someone later cut, rearranged and mounted as a pair of screens because they recognised its quality.

Not everyone agrees on the details. Scholars disagree about what the study was for and how much the mounting has changed the composition, and some resist calling it a mere sketch at all. The attribution to Tōhaku is broadly accepted on the evidence of the brushwork, but the documentation is thin.

This bears on how we look at it. A large part of what modern viewers admire in the Pine Trees is its restraint: the sense that the painter knew exactly when to stop. If the screens are a draft, some of that restraint may be incompleteness, so that the emptiness we praise may partly be paper that was never meant to stay blank. Alternatively, the freedom of a private study, made without a patron watching, may be exactly what let Tōhaku paint with such speed and looseness. Both views are interpretations, and the physical evidence supports either.

Other interpretations have built up around the screens, and they need to be kept separate from the evidence.

The first is about grief. Tōhaku's son Kyūzō, the painter of the Chishaku-in cherry blossoms and evidently a major talent, died in 1593 at about the age of twenty-five. Because the Pine Trees screens are usually dated to the same years, some writers have read them as a work of mourning, with the father turning away from gold to a grey, quiet world of fog. It is a moving idea and it may be true, but no document connects the screens to Kyūzō's death, and the dating is not precise enough to prove the link. It is best treated as a possibility that the screens make easy to believe, not as a fact.

The second is about home. Tōhaku grew up on a coast lined with pines and often hung with sea mist. Some writers suggest that the screens remember Noto, a landscape from childhood painted from memory in the capital. Again, nothing documents this. In Japanese art, pines in mist are a widely shared subject and do not have to come from one particular place.

The third concerns a Japanese idea usually rendered as *ma*. The word means an interval or gap, the space or pause between things. It is used of rooms, of timing in music and theatre, and of conversation. It is often invoked in writing about the Pine Trees, because the empty paper between the clusters seems as deliberate as the trees. The concept is real and old, but much of the modern writing that presents *ma* as a single key to "the Japanese aesthetic" dates from the twentieth century, some of it aimed at Western audiences. It is a useful lens. It does not prove what Tōhaku had in mind.

What can be said without speculation is narrower. In the screens, the white of the paper does several jobs at once. Between the clusters it reads as fog. Around the trunks it reads as light. At the top of the left screen it reads as snow on a mountain. Underfoot it reads as ground hidden by mist. It is often invoked in writing about the Pine Trees, because the empty paper between the clusters seems as deliberate as the trees. The concept is real and old, but much of the modern writing that presents *ma* as a single key to "the Japanese aesthetic" dates from the twentieth century, some of it aimed at Western audiences. It is a useful lens. It does not prove what Tōhaku had in mind.

What can be said without speculation is narrower. In the screens, the white of the paper does several jobs at once. Between the clusters it reads as fog. Around the trunks it reads as light. At the top of the left screen it reads as snow on a mountain. Underfoot it reads as ground hidden by mist. The same unchanged surface is read as four different things depending on what the ink around it implies. That is a precise technical achievement, and it is why the emptiness doesn't feel empty.

The pine also has its own associations in East Asian art. It is evergreen, and it was a standard emblem of endurance, longevity and steadfastness, as well as a fixture of the New Year. Pine decorations called *kadomatsu* still stand beside Japanese doorways at the turn of the year. That is one reason the museum's January showing feels right, though it is a modern custom, not something Tōhaku arranged.

## Seeing more by being shown less

Tōhaku lived for many years after the screens were painted. He kept working, kept competing with the Kanō, and kept claiming his descent from Sesshū. In 1610, at about seventy-one, he travelled to Edo, the new seat of the Tokugawa shoguns, apparently at their summons. He fell ill on the journey and died shortly after arriving. His workshop, the Hasegawa school, continued after him but never matched the Kanō's institutional power. For long periods Tōhaku was remembered as one capable painter among several.

The Pine Trees screens became famous largely in the twentieth century, as Japanese and foreign critics took up ink painting, Zen and understatement as defining Japanese values. The screens fit that story almost too well, and some caution is due. The twentieth century made them a national emblem. Tōhaku's own century, as far as we know, did not single them out.

They have lasted, though, and there is a reason for that apart from fashion. A gold screen by Eitoku tells you what to see and leaves you impressed. The Pine Trees screens supply only part of the picture and let the viewer's eye complete it. The fog is the viewer's own inference from a few gradations of ink, and the mountain is barely more than a suggestion. The painting works because the eye keeps filling in what it was not given, and the screens trust it to do so.

Whether Tōhaku meant them as a sketch or a statement, they raise a question worth keeping in mind on an ordinary day: when an artist leaves something out, how much of what we then see was put there by the artist, and how much by us?
key_ideas: Hasegawa Tōhaku's Pine Trees screens (1590s) create fog almost entirely from unpainted paper, using darker and paler ink to make some pines seem near and others far.
The screens were painted during the Momoyama period, when the prevailing taste, led by Kanō Eitoku and his school, favored bold trees on gold-leaf grounds for warlords' castles.
Tōhaku drew on the Chinese monk-painter Muqi and claimed descent from Sesshū, using these lineages to compete as an outsider against the hereditary Kanō workshop.
Coarse paper, misaligned panel joins, and seals thought to be later additions lead many scholars to believe the screens were a preparatory study rather than a finished commission.
Readings of the screens as mourning for Tōhaku's son Kyūzō or as memories of his native Noto coast are attractive interpretations without documentary proof.

glossary.definition: A Japanese folding screen of hinged panels, often made in pairs and stood in a zigzag on the floor to divide or decorate a room.
The era of Japan's reunification under Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, roughly the last quarter of the sixteenth century, known for castles and lavish gold-ground painting.
A hereditary family workshop of painters that dominated official Japanese painting for centuries, led in the late 1500s by Kanō Eitoku.
East Asian ink made from soot and glue, ground with water to give tones from deep black to the palest grey.
Sliding doors or wall panels in Japanese architecture, often painted, which formed the main surface for large-scale interior paintings.
A Japanese concept of interval or meaningful gap, the space or pause between things, often invoked in discussions of empty areas in art.
A short record of Hasegawa Tōhaku's remarks on painting and earlier masters, written down by the Nichiren priest Nittsū.
